nodeData.note: Technical track · The ML workflow, supervised and unsupervised learning, evaluation and overfitting, classic algorithms.

children.note: Machine learning projects follow a repeating cycle: frame the problem, prepare data, build features, split, train, evaluate, deploy and monitor. Good process matters as much as clever algorithms.

Supervised learning trains a model on examples with known answers so it can predict answers for new inputs. It covers regression (numbers) and classification (categories) and is the most widely deployed kind of machine learning.

Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data: groups of similar items, compact summaries of many features, and unusual points. Self-supervised learning extends the idea by making labels from the data itself.

How to measure whether a model truly works on new data: confusion matrices, precision and recall, ROC-AUC and cross-validation. It also covers why models overfit and how regularisation and leakage-free splits keep results honest.

The workhorse algorithms of machine learning: decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, SVMs, k-nearest neighbours and naive Bayes. Each has strengths and weaknesses, and knowing when to use which is a core skill.

nodeData.note: Machine learning projects follow a repeating cycle: frame the problem, prepare data, build features, split, train, evaluate, deploy and monitor. Good process matters as much as clever algorithms.

children.note: A machine learning project is a loop, not a single training run. You frame a problem, prepare data, train and evaluate a model, ship it, then watch it and return to earlier steps when things change.
Real projects jump back often: poor evaluation sends you to fix data, and drift after launch sends you to retrain. Plan for iteration from the start.

manas.q: Why is the ML workflow described as a loop rather than a straight line?

children.note: Practitioners commonly report that collecting, cleaning and understanding data takes far more effort than choosing or training the model itself.

children.topic: Model code is a small part
children.note: A well-known 2015 NeurIPS paper on hidden technical debt argued that the learning code is a small box inside a much larger system of data pipelines, configuration, serving and monitoring.
MLOps applies DevOps habits (automation, versioning, continuous delivery) to ML so models can be deployed and maintained reliably in production.

manas.q: What is MLOps?

children.note: Before touching data, decide exactly what to predict, for whom, and how success will be judged. A vague goal produces a model nobody uses.
Write the output precisely: for example 'will this M-Pesa merchant miss a loan repayment within 30 days?' rather than 'find risky customers'.
Is the answer a number (regression), a category (classification), a ranking, or groups with no labels (clustering)? The type decides the methods and metrics.

manas.q: Name four common ML task types.

children.note: Agree on what matters in the real world, such as money saved or patients correctly referred, then pick an ML metric that tracks it.
Record how well a simple rule or the current human process does. A model is only useful if it clearly beats this baseline.

manas.q: Why measure a simple baseline before building a model?

children.note: If a few clear rules solve the problem, or there is too little data, ordinary software may be cheaper, safer and easier to explain.
Gather examples that represent the situations the model will face, then fix errors, gaps and inconsistencies. Garbage in, garbage out.
Databases, sensors, surveys, logs, public datasets or newly labelled examples. Note who collected each source, when, and under what consent.
For supervised learning each example needs the correct answer. Labels from tired or untrained annotators add noise that caps model quality.

manas.q: Why does label quality limit model quality?

children.note: Data from Nairobi clinics alone may not reflect rural Turkana or rural Bihar. If a group is missing in training, the model is likely to fail for that group.
Options include dropping rows, filling with a median or a 'missing' flag, or using models that handle gaps. Always ask why the value is missing.
Remove repeated records, impossible values (age 250) and inconsistent units. Duplicates across train and test also inflate scores.
Plot distributions, check class balance and look at random rows by eye. Exploratory analysis catches problems no metric will.
Personal data is covered by laws such as Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 and the EU GDPR. Collect only what you need; check the current text for duties.
Features are the input columns the model sees. Turning raw data into informative, well-scaled features often improves results more than switching algorithms.
One measurable property of an example, such as rainfall last month, crop type or patient age. The full set forms the input vector x.

manas.q: What is a feature in machine learning?

children.note: Models need numbers. One-hot encoding turns 'county = Kisumu' into a column of 0s and 1s for each county.
Standardising (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) puts features on similar ranges, which matters for k-NN, SVMs and gradient descent.
Combine raw columns into meaningful ones, such as debt-to-income ratio or days since last purchase. Domain knowledge is the key ingredient.
Compute scaling means, encodings and imputation values from the training set, then apply them to validation and test, or information leaks.

manas.q: Why must preprocessing statistics be computed on the training set only?

children.note: Libraries bundle preprocessing and model into one object so the same steps run identically in training and in production.
In scikit-learn: pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()); pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) - the scaler learns from training data only.
Hold some data back so you can measure performance on examples the model has never seen. This is the only honest estimate of real-world quality.
Used to fit the model's parameters, such as regression weights. The model sees these examples directly.

manas.q: What is the training set used for?

children.note: Used to compare models and tune hyperparameters like tree depth. Because you make choices on it, its score becomes slightly optimistic.

manas.q: What is the validation set used for?

children.note: Kept locked away and used once at the end to report final performance. Reusing it to tune turns it into another validation set.

manas.q: Why should the test set be used only once?

children.note: Splits like 70/15/15 or 80/10/10 are common starting points; with millions of examples a small fraction is enough for validation and test.
For forecasting, train on the past and test on the future. If one patient has many records, keep all of them on the same side of the split.
Stratified splitting keeps the class mix (say 5% fraud) the same in every set, so rare classes are not missing from validation.
Training searches for parameter values that make predictions match labels on the training set, usually by minimising a loss function.
A number that measures how wrong the predictions are, for example mean squared error: loss = mean of (y − ŷ)². Training tries to make it small.

manas.q: What does a loss function measure?

children.note: Repeatedly nudge each parameter a small step in the direction that reduces the loss most steeply; the step size is the learning rate.

manas.q: What does gradient descent do?

children.note: Parameters are learned from data (weights). Hyperparameters are chosen by you before training (learning rate, number of trees, k in k-NN).

manas.q: What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?

children.note: Grid search, random search or Bayesian optimisation try many hyperparameter settings and keep the one with the best validation score.
Log data version, code version, settings and scores for every run so results can be reproduced and compared later.
Judge the model on held-out data with metrics that reflect the real goal, and look beyond one average number.
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data; use precision, recall, F1 or AUC for classification and MAE or RMSE for regression.
Report the gain over the simple baseline from step 1. A 92% accurate model is weak if always guessing the majority class gives 91%.
Read through the wrong predictions and group them. Patterns such as blurry photos or one region often point to the next data fix.
Check performance separately for gender, region, language or device. A good average can hide poor results for a minority group.

manas.q: Why check model performance on subgroups, not just overall?

children.note: Put the model where it can make predictions for real users or systems, with safeguards around it.
Batch scoring runs on a schedule (nightly risk scores); online serving answers each request in milliseconds through an API.

manas.q: What is the difference between batch and online prediction?

children.note: Small models can run on phones or devices without internet, useful for crop-disease apps used in fields with weak signal.
Run the new model silently beside the old one, or on a small share of traffic, before switching everyone over.
For high-stakes uses such as medicine or credit, let the model assist a trained person rather than decide alone.
Keep every model version with its data and code so you can return to the last good one quickly if problems appear.
After launch the world keeps changing, so a model that was good last year can quietly get worse. Monitoring catches this early.
The input distribution shifts, for example new phone models or a new customer region, even if the underlying relationship stays the same.

manas.q: What is data drift?

children.note: The relationship between inputs and the target changes over time, such as fraud patterns adapting to detection, making old predictions wrong.

manas.q: What is concept drift?

children.note: Input statistics, prediction distribution, latency, errors and, when labels arrive later, true accuracy over time.
Retrain on fresh data on a schedule or when monitored metrics cross a threshold, then evaluate again before redeploying.
A model's own predictions can change future data, for example only approved applicants generate repayment labels. Plan for this bias.
Most ML failures come from process errors, not from the choice of algorithm.
Information about the answer sneaks into training features or the split, giving great test scores that collapse in real use.

manas.q: What is data leakage?

children.note: Peeking at test results while making choices makes the final score too optimistic.
Teams sometimes build a complex model that barely beats a simple rule and costs much more to run.
Shipping and forgetting a model lets drift silently cause harm for months.
If the target itself is biased or poorly chosen, a more accurate model simply reproduces that problem more efficiently.
Short and long videos that walk through the workflow and its steps.

nodeData.note: Supervised learning trains a model on examples with known answers so it can predict answers for new inputs. It covers regression (numbers) and classification (categories) and is the most widely deployed kind of machine learning.

children.note: Supervised learning learns a function from inputs to outputs using examples where the correct output (the label) is known.
Each training example is a pair (x, y): x is the input features, y the correct answer. The model learns a mapping f so that f(x) ≈ y.

manas.q: What does each supervised training example contain?

children.note: The labels act like a teacher marking answers, telling the algorithm how wrong each prediction was.
Fitting the training data is easy; the real aim is accurate predictions on new, unseen examples.

manas.q: What is the real goal of supervised learning?

children.note: Someone must provide the answers, such as doctors marking X-rays or agronomists naming leaf diseases, so labelled data is often the bottleneck.
Combines a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one, useful when labels are scarce but raw data is plentiful.
The two main supervised tasks differ in the kind of answer they predict.
Predicts a continuous number, such as maize yield in tonnes per hectare, house price in rupees or tomorrow's temperature.

manas.q: What kind of output does regression predict?

children.note: Predicts a category, such as spam or not spam, disease present or absent, or which of 10 digits is written.

manas.q: What kind of output does classification predict?

children.note: Binary has two classes; multiclass has more than two (crop type); multilabel lets one example carry several labels at once (a photo with a cow and a goat).

manas.q: How do binary, multiclass and multilabel classification differ?

children.note: Many classifiers output a probability per class; a threshold such as 0.5 turns it into a decision, and the threshold can be moved.
'How many days late will this loan be?' is regression; 'Will it be more than 30 days late?' is classification. The framing is a choice.
The simplest regression model: predict the output as a weighted sum of the inputs plus a constant.
ŷ = w1·x1 + w2·x2 + … + b. Each weight w says how much the prediction changes when that feature goes up by one unit.

manas.q: What is the form of a linear regression prediction?

children.note: Classic linear regression picks weights that minimise the sum of squared errors between predictions and true values.

manas.q: What does ordinary least squares minimise?

children.note: Small problems can be solved exactly with linear algebra; very large ones are often fitted iteratively with gradient descent.
Weights are easy to read and explain, which is one reason linear models remain common in economics, medicine and policy.
It assumes a straight-line relationship; curved patterns need transformed features (x²) or a more flexible model. It is also sensitive to outliers.
Adding x², x³ or products of features lets a linear model fit curves while staying linear in its weights.

manas.q: How can linear regression fit a curved relationship?

children.note: In scikit-learn: model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train); model.predict(X_new) returns predicted numbers.
Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification model. It turns a linear score into a probability between 0 and 1.
p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), where z = w·x + b. The sigmoid squashes any number into the range 0 to 1.

manas.q: What does the sigmoid function do in logistic regression?

children.note: The model is linear in the log-odds: log(p / (1 − p)) = w·x + b. Each weight shifts the odds by a fixed factor.
Predicting class 1 when p ≥ 0.5 means the boundary between classes is a straight line (or flat plane) in feature space.
Softmax regression extends the idea to many classes by producing a probability for each class that sums to 1.
Fast, stable and explainable, it is a common first model for credit scoring, clinical risk scores and text classification.
A loss function scores how wrong a prediction is. Training means finding parameters that make the average loss small.
MSE = mean of (y − ŷ)². Squaring punishes big errors heavily; it is the standard regression loss.

manas.q: What is the formula for mean squared error?

children.note: MAE = mean of |y − ŷ|. Less sensitive to outliers than MSE, and its value is in the same units as the target.
For classification: loss = −[y·log(p) + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)]. Confident wrong answers are punished very strongly.

manas.q: Which loss is standard for logistic regression and classifiers?

children.note: Used by support vector machines; it is zero when a point is on the correct side with a safe margin and grows linearly otherwise.
The loss is what the optimiser minimises; the metric (accuracy, F1, RMSE) is what you report. They are related but not always the same.
Supervised models are fitted by searching for parameters that minimise loss on the training data.
w ← w − η·∂loss/∂w. Move each weight a little against the slope of the loss; η is the learning rate.

manas.q: What is the gradient descent update rule?

children.note: Too large and training overshoots or diverges; too small and it crawls. It is one of the most important hyperparameters.

manas.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large or too small?

children.note: Computing the gradient on small random batches instead of the whole dataset is much faster and works well in practice.
A flexible model can memorise training labels, including their noise, and then do poorly on new data. Validation data reveals this.
Supervised learning powers most deployed ML systems today.
Image classifiers trained on labelled leaf pictures can flag diseases such as cassava mosaic, helping farmers act early.
Mobile lenders in Kenya and India use classifiers on repayment and transaction history to estimate default risk, which raises fairness questions.
Models predict outcomes such as readmission or diabetic eye disease from records or scans, usually as support for clinicians.
Email and payment systems classify messages and transactions as normal or suspicious, retraining often as attackers adapt.
Regression models predict sales, electricity load or hospital admissions so organisations can plan stock and staff.
Supervised learning is powerful but only as good as its labels, data and framing.
Collecting accurate labels is slow and costly, especially in specialist areas such as pathology or local languages.
If past decisions were unfair, a model trained to copy them learns the same unfairness.

manas.q: Why can supervised models repeat historical bias?

children.note: A model can predict well using features that merely correlate with the outcome; it does not tell you what would happen if you intervened.
Performance can drop sharply when deployed on a population or time period unlike the training data.
When one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy while missing nearly every rare case; use suitable metrics and resampling.
Clear video explanations of the core ideas.

nodeData.note: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data: groups of similar items, compact summaries of many features, and unusual points. Self-supervised learning extends the idea by making labels from the data itself.

children.note: Unsupervised learning looks for structure in data that has no labels: groups, directions of variation, or unusual points.
Only inputs x are available, with no target y. The algorithm must find patterns on its own.

manas.q: What is the key difference between unsupervised and supervised data?

children.note: Clustering (grouping similar items), dimensionality reduction (compressing features) and anomaly detection (spotting the unusual).

manas.q: Name three main unsupervised learning tasks.

children.note: Unlabelled data is cheap and plentiful. Unsupervised methods help explore it, summarise it and prepare features for later supervised models.
With no correct answers, judging whether the found structure is 'right' needs domain experts, internal scores or a downstream task.
Clustering partitions data so items in the same group are more similar to each other than to items in other groups.
Splits data into k groups, each represented by its centre (centroid), by minimising the squared distance from points to their centre.
Pick k starting centres; assign each point to its nearest centre; move each centre to the mean of its points; repeat until stable.

manas.q: What are the two repeated steps of k-means?

children.note: You must set k yourself. The elbow plot (error vs k) and silhouette score help, but domain sense matters most.

manas.q: Who decides the number of clusters in k-means?

children.note: Results depend on the starting centres, it assumes roughly round, similar-sized clusters, and it needs scaled features.
In scikit-learn: km = KMeans(n_clusters=4).fit(X); km.labels_ gives each point's cluster.
Builds a tree of nested clusters instead of a single flat split.
Start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one remains.

manas.q: How does agglomerative clustering work?

children.note: A tree diagram of the merges. Cutting it at a chosen height gives any number of clusters without rerunning.

manas.q: What is a dendrogram?

children.note: How 'closest clusters' is measured (single, complete, average or Ward linkage) changes the shapes of clusters found.
Standard methods slow down badly on very large datasets, so they suit thousands rather than millions of points.
A density-based method that finds clusters of any shape as dense regions and labels isolated points as noise; no k needed.
Clustering depends on how similarity is measured. Unscaled features let one large-range column dominate the result.
Many datasets have hundreds of features. Reduction methods find a few new coordinates that keep most of the useful information.
To visualise data in 2D or 3D, remove noise and redundancy, speed up later models and ease the 'curse of dimensionality'.

manas.q: Give two reasons to reduce dimensionality.

children.note: Principal component analysis finds new axes, ordered by how much variance in the data they capture, and keeps the top few.
Each component is a weighted mix of original features; the first points along the direction of greatest spread.

manas.q: What does the first principal component capture?

children.note: Each component reports the share of total variance it explains, helping decide how many to keep.
PCA can only rotate and project; it cannot unfold curved structure. It is fast, deterministic and a good first step.
A nonlinear method for 2D or 3D maps that keeps points which are close in high dimensions close on the map.
It is excellent at showing clusters, which is why it became popular for single-cell biology and word embeddings.
Distances between clusters and cluster sizes on a t-SNE plot are not reliable, and results change with the perplexity setting.

manas.q: Which features of a t-SNE plot should not be over-interpreted?

children.note: Uniform manifold approximation and projection is a newer nonlinear method, usually faster than t-SNE and often keeps more global layout.
A widely cited 2018 Nature Biotechnology paper showed UMAP visualising single-cell data quickly and clearly.
Like t-SNE, its picture depends on settings, and apparent gaps or distances should be checked with other methods.
Neural networks trained to compress input into a small code and rebuild it; the code acts as a learned low-dimensional representation.
Finds rare items that differ strongly from the bulk of the data, often without labelled examples of what 'bad' looks like.
Card or mobile-money fraud, faulty machine sensors, network intrusions and unusual lab results.

manas.q: Name two common uses of anomaly detection.

children.note: Simple methods flag values far from the mean (for example beyond 3 standard deviations) or outside the interquartile range.
Builds random trees that split data at random; anomalies get isolated in very few splits, so short paths mean 'unusual'.

manas.q: Why do anomalies get short paths in an isolation forest?

children.note: Points in sparse regions or far from their nearest neighbours (as in local outlier factor) are scored as anomalies.
An autoencoder trained on normal data rebuilds normal inputs well and unusual ones poorly; high error suggests an anomaly.
A flagged point may be a data error, a fraud, or simply a new but legitimate behaviour. Humans must review alerts.
A middle ground where the data supplies its own labels, letting models learn from huge unlabelled collections.
Hide part of the input and train the model to predict it. The hidden part becomes a free label created from the data itself.

manas.q: Where do the labels come from in self-supervised learning?

children.note: Large language models such as GPT-style models and Claude are pretrained largely by predicting the next token in vast amounts of text.
BERT-style models learn by guessing words that were blanked out of a sentence; vision models can do the same with image patches.
Two altered views of the same image are pulled together in representation space while views of different images are pushed apart.
Representations learned this way are then adapted with a small labelled set, which cuts the labelling needed for a new task.

manas.q: Why does self-supervised pretraining reduce the need for labels?

children.note: Unsupervised methods are often a first step in understanding data.
A retailer or SACCO can cluster members by spending and saving patterns to design better products for each group.
Researchers cluster and map thousands of cells by gene activity to discover cell types, using PCA, t-SNE and UMAP.
Grouping news articles or patient complaints by similar wording reveals themes without reading every document first.
Clustering pixel values can separate water, forest, cropland and bare soil as a starting point for land-use maps.
Unsupervised results are easy to produce and easy to over-read.
Algorithms like k-means will return k groups even from random data. Check that clusters are stable and meaningful.

manas.q: Why should you be careful trusting clusters from k-means?

children.note: Different feature choices or scaling can produce completely different clusters from the same records.
2D maps from t-SNE or UMAP can suggest separations that do not exist in the original data.
Without labels, success often means 'useful to an expert', which takes time and judgement to establish.

nodeData.note: How to measure whether a model truly works on new data: confusion matrices, precision and recall, ROC-AUC and cross-validation. It also covers why models overfit and how regularisation and leakage-free splits keep results honest.

children.note: A model is useful only if it works on data it has never seen. Evaluation estimates that, and choosing the wrong metric can hide serious failures.
The ability to perform well on new examples from the same kind of source, not just on the training set.

manas.q: What is generalisation in machine learning?

children.note: A model can score near 100% on training data by memorising it; only held-out data shows real skill.
Missing a cancer is worse than a false alarm; blocking a genuine M-Pesa payment annoys customers. The costs of errors decide the metric.
A table counting predictions against true classes. Most classification metrics are built from its four cells.
True positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN), for a chosen positive class.

manas.q: What are the four cells of a binary confusion matrix?

children.note: Predicting positive when the truth is negative, such as flagging a healthy person as ill.
Predicting negative when the truth is positive, such as missing a person who really has TB.

manas.q: What is a false negative?

children.note: With many classes the matrix is k × k; off-diagonal cells show which classes the model confuses with each other.
Different summaries of the confusion matrix answer different questions.
accuracy = (TP + TN) / all. Simple, but misleading when classes are imbalanced.
If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that always says 'not fraud' is 99% accurate yet catches nothing.

manas.q: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?

children.note: precision = TP / (TP + FP). Of the cases flagged positive, how many really were? High precision means few false alarms.

manas.q: What is the formula for precision?

children.note: recall = TP / (TP + FN). Of all real positives, how many did we catch? Screening programmes value high recall.

manas.q: What is the formula for recall?

children.note: specificity = TN / (TN + FP). Of all real negatives, how many were correctly cleared? Common in medical test reporting.
F1 = 2·precision·recall / (precision + recall), the harmonic mean. It is high only when both precision and recall are high.

manas.q: What does the F1 score combine, and how?

children.note: Raising the decision threshold usually increases precision and lowers recall; lowering it does the reverse.
For numeric targets use MAE (average absolute error), RMSE (root mean squared error) or R² (share of variance explained).
Tools for judging a classifier across all possible thresholds, not just one.
Plots true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate (1 − specificity) as the threshold moves from strict to lenient.

manas.q: What two rates does a ROC curve plot?

children.note: Area under the ROC curve: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is no better than random guessing.

manas.q: What AUC value means no better than random?

children.note: AUC equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative.
When positives are very rare, the PR curve and its area are often more informative than ROC-AUC.
AUC summarises ranking quality, but deployment needs one threshold chosen from the real costs of each error type.
The central tension in ML: a model must be flexible enough to learn the pattern but not so flexible that it learns the noise.
The model fits training data, including random noise, too closely and does worse on new data. Low training error, high validation error.

manas.q: What is overfitting?

children.note: The model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does poorly on both training and validation data.

manas.q: What is underfitting?

children.note: Plot training and validation error as data or training time grows; a widening gap signals overfitting.
A student who memorises past papers word for word fails new questions; one who learns the ideas handles them. Models are the same.
Prediction error on new data can be split into bias, variance and irreducible noise.
Error from overly simple assumptions, like fitting a straight line to a curve. High bias leads to underfitting.

manas.q: What does high bias usually cause?

children.note: Error from sensitivity to the particular training sample; a high-variance model changes a lot if trained on slightly different data.

manas.q: What does high variance usually cause?

children.note: More complex models usually lower bias but raise variance. The best test error is often at a middle complexity.
Noise in the data itself that no model can remove, such as measurement error or factors not recorded.
Very large neural networks can generalise well despite having more parameters than examples, a pattern studied as 'double descent'.
A way to get a steadier estimate of performance by training and validating several times on different splits.
Split the data into k parts; train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining one, rotating k times, then average the scores.

manas.q: How does k-fold cross-validation work?

children.note: k = 5 or k = 10 are typical. Leave-one-out uses k equal to the number of examples and is costly.
Stratified folds keep class balance; grouped folds keep all records of one patient or farm in the same fold.
For data ordered in time, always validate on periods after the training period, never before.
An inner loop tunes hyperparameters and an outer loop measures performance, avoiding optimistic bias from tuning.
In scikit-learn: cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5) returns five validation scores to average.
Techniques that discourage needless complexity so the model generalises better.
Adds λ·Σw² to the loss, shrinking all weights towards zero but rarely to exactly zero.

manas.q: What penalty does L2 (ridge) regularisation add?

children.note: Adds λ·Σ|w| to the loss, which can push some weights exactly to zero and so selects features.

manas.q: Which regularisation can set weights exactly to zero?

children.note: A mix of L1 and L2 penalties, useful when many features are correlated.
λ is a hyperparameter tuned on validation data: too high underfits, too low allows overfitting.
Early stopping, dropout in neural networks, pruning trees, limiting depth and simply collecting more data all reduce overfitting.
Leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time slips into training, giving scores that are too good to be true.
A feature secretly encodes the answer, for example 'treatment given' when predicting the diagnosis that triggered the treatment.

manas.q: What is target leakage?

children.note: Duplicates or near-duplicates in both sets, or scaling fitted on all data before splitting, let test information leak in.
Using future information to predict the past, such as random splits on stock prices or disease outbreaks.
Images from the same patient in both train and test let the model recognise the patient rather than the disease.

Split first, fit all preprocessing inside the training fold, split by time or group where needed, and distrust surprisingly high scores.

nodeData.note: The workhorse algorithms of machine learning: decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, SVMs, k-nearest neighbours and naive Bayes. Each has strengths and weaknesses, and knowing when to use which is a core skill.

children.note: Before and alongside deep learning, a small set of well-understood algorithms solves most problems with tables of data. They are fast, cheap and often hard to beat.
On spreadsheet-style data (rows of customers, patients, farms) tree ensembles such as gradient boosting frequently match or beat neural networks.

manas.q: Which family often wins on tabular data?

children.note: The no free lunch theorems say no single method is best for every possible problem, so you compare candidates on your own data.

manas.q: What does the 'no free lunch' idea imply for choosing algorithms?

children.note: Many run on a laptop in seconds and are easier to inspect than large neural networks, which matters in regulated fields.
A tree of yes/no questions on features that ends in a prediction at each leaf, like a flowchart learned from data.
At each node the algorithm picks the feature and threshold that best separate the classes, measured by Gini impurity or entropy.

manas.q: What measures are used to choose decision tree splits?

children.note: For numeric targets each leaf predicts the average value of its training examples, and splits reduce squared error.
A shallow tree can be printed and followed by a doctor or loan officer, such as 'if age > 60 and BP > 140 then high risk'.
A deep tree can create a leaf for nearly every example. Limit depth, require minimum leaf size or prune.

manas.q: Why do single deep decision trees overfit?

children.note: Trees compare one feature at a time against a threshold, so they do not need standardised features.
An ensemble of many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of rows and features; their votes are combined.
Bootstrap aggregating: train each tree on a random sample drawn with replacement, then average or vote.

manas.q: What is bagging?

children.note: At each split only a random subset of features is considered, which makes trees less alike and the ensemble stronger.
Individual trees have high variance; averaging many partly independent trees cancels much of that variance.

manas.q: Why does averaging many trees help a random forest?

children.note: Rows left out of a tree's sample act as a built-in validation set, giving a free performance estimate.
Forests report which features most reduced error, a useful but imperfect guide, as correlated features share credit.
Works well with little tuning on many tabular problems, making it a strong first model.
Builds trees one after another, each new small tree correcting the errors left by the trees before it.
Each new tree is trained on the remaining errors (more precisely, the gradient of the loss), then added with a small weight.

manas.q: What does each new tree learn in gradient boosting?

children.note: A smaller learning rate with more trees usually generalises better but trains longer; early stopping picks the count.
An open-source library for fast, regularised gradient boosting that became famous for winning many data-science competitions.

manas.q: What is XGBoost?

children.note: Other popular boosting libraries; LightGBM is designed for speed on large data, CatBoost for handling categorical features.
Bagging trains trees independently to reduce variance; boosting trains them in sequence to reduce bias.

manas.q: How does boosting differ from bagging?

children.note: Depth, learning rate, number of trees and regularisation interact; untuned boosting can overfit noisy data.
SVMs find the boundary that separates classes with the widest possible margin.
Among all separating lines or planes, choose the one with the largest gap to the nearest points of each class.

manas.q: What does an SVM try to maximise?

children.note: The training points closest to the boundary; they alone determine where it lies.
Kernels such as polynomial or RBF let an SVM draw curved boundaries by implicitly working in a higher-dimensional space.

manas.q: What does the kernel trick allow an SVM to do?

children.note: The C hyperparameter trades margin width against training mistakes; small C tolerates more errors for a smoother boundary.
Strong on small to medium datasets with many features, such as text, but slow on millions of rows and needs scaled inputs.
Predicts by looking at the k most similar training examples and taking their majority class or average value.
There is no real training step; all work happens at prediction time by searching for neighbours.

manas.q: Why is k-NN called a lazy learner?

children.note: Small k follows noise (overfits); large k blurs boundaries (underfits). Pick k with cross-validation.
Uses a distance such as Euclidean, so features must be scaled or one large-range feature dominates.
With many features, all points become roughly equally far apart, and 'nearest' neighbours stop being meaningful.

manas.q: Why does k-NN struggle with many features?

children.note: In scikit-learn: KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_new).
A fast probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem with a strong simplifying assumption.
P(class | features) ∝ P(features | class) · P(class): update a prior belief using evidence from the features.
Treats every feature as independent of the others within a class, which is rarely true but makes it very fast.

manas.q: What is 'naive' about naive Bayes?

children.note: Works surprisingly well for spam filtering and sorting messages by topic, even in Swahili or Hindi, with little data.
Multinomial for word counts, Bernoulli for yes/no features, Gaussian for continuous measurements.
It often ranks classes well, but its probability values tend to be overconfident.
A practical guide; always confirm with validation on your own data.
Begin with linear or logistic regression as a baseline, then try a random forest and a gradient boosting model.

manas.q: What is a sensible order for trying classic models on a new tabular problem?

children.note: Prefer logistic regression or a shallow decision tree when decisions must be justified to patients, borrowers or regulators.
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) is usually the strongest choice when tuned with care.
SVMs and regularised linear models suit datasets with few rows but many features, such as gene expression.
Naive Bayes or logistic regression on word counts are fast, strong baselines.
For raw unstructured data, deep neural networks have largely replaced classic algorithms.
k-NN suits small datasets and recommendation-style 'find similar' tasks if features are well scaled.
Common errors when using classic algorithms.
Forgetting to scale features ruins k-NN and SVM results while trees are unaffected.
Feature importance shows what the model used, not what causes the outcome.
Tuning many hyperparameters against the test set produces optimistic scores; use cross-validation.
Scores from boosting, SVMs and naive Bayes may not be true probabilities; calibrate if you need them.
